r8-m01.abandon: m01 needs the early errors that RL avoids (misreadings and slips, located at a median 0.20 of the answer) to become less likely when the base samples at a lower temperature. The board already says the reverse. (1) result-faf15a measured the base's own located wrong steps and found they are not low-probability draws: "Under the base the wrong step has log-prob -0.53 per token vs -0.63 for control text (W4 refuted): truncation or low temperature cannot remove these steps", and "the base's wrong step is not an unlikely sample". The same item names these as exactly the errors RL removes: "RL lowers misreadings and slips, not wrong plans". (2) knowledge-16c62a, which closes the decoding-time routes, says it directly: "T 0.6 raises the wrong steps." (3) result-afc423 puts these steps early ("First wrong step at median 0.20 of the answer"), which is the window where m01 places T 0.6. facts.json backs this up: the r7-m05 cause test found that rescoring at T 0.6 raises the wrong step relative to control text in 0.608 of the 51 items. A sharper distribution therefore favours the base's early wrong step instead of avoiding it, and that removes the cause the position switch relies on. m01's own starting observation does not rescue it. In knowledge-13cff3 ('on the 402 problems that finish at T 0.6, T 1.0 gets only 361-364 against 378') the problems are picked by whether the T 0.6 sample finished. That drops T 0.6's failed draws but not T 1.0's, so it does not show T 0.6 choosing better early. The one paired, symmetric comparison of finished answers (the egate lo6 fact, +0.017 lower error) covers confident tokens over the whole answer, not an early segment. result-34897a adds that sharpening any regime brings cap hits back: 'Cap hits per 500: T 1.0 22.5, forks only 33, confident only 44'. A T 0.6 opening is therefore expected to add loops and wrong early steps, not to give the 418-424 that m01 predicts.

r8-m03.abandon: The board already measured what m03 predicts and found the opposite. m03 says misreadings happen because the cued base does not copy the problem's givens word for word near the start of its answer, so it later reads them from its own paraphrase. A verbatim restatement in the early text shows up as high problem dependence: log p(token | problem) - log p(token | no problem), averaged over the first 1,000 tokens. This is large on copied tokens. About 80 copied tokens at a few nats each would move the 1,000-token mean by about 0.2 nats, more than the gaps between labels. result-f3d708 computed this quantity for all 2,000 stored cued-base samples. (1) Misread samples are not the least problem-dependent: "Predictions P1 and P3 refuted: misread samples do not have the lowest value (0.132 nats per token; slip 0.094, wrong plan 0.154)." So misread answers depend on the problem text more than slip answers do, not less. (2) Right and wrong siblings of the same problem do not differ: the statistic "ranks the right sample above the wrong one of the same problem in 53.1 % of pairs [46.8, 58.9]; chance is 50." Under m03, right siblings should carry the restatement that wrong siblings lack. knowledge-16c62a lists this test among the closed routes: "problem dependence log p(tok|problem) - log p(tok|no problem) 0.531 [0.468, 0.589] (result-f3d708)". The early setup in result-c495fe ("a misreading starts before its sentence") is still real, but the in-context-copy cause m03 gives for it is contradicted. Also, the facts.json r7-m05 numbers show that deleting the problem raises misread and wrong-plan steps alike (0.686 vs 0.688), which does not single out misreadings as a failure to read the givens. m03's proposed coverage statistic would mostly re-measure what f3d708 already found to be null.

r8-m04.abandon: m04 says the RL-written examples work by giving the base a prior over answer length (and closing habit), so that it writes longer answers and stops giving quick finished-wrong ones. It explains draw 2's null by saying draw 2's examples were shorter or less checked. The board already rules out that account. (1) Draw 2 moved the base's output length as much as draw 1 did, yet gained nothing. result-6d422d gives draw 1 as '435/497 tokens 4400 | cue + 3 examples written by Math-RL in context'. result-5227b9 gives draw 2 as 'score: base MATH-500 401/494 tokens 4361 | cue + 3 examples written by Math-RL in context (draw 2)', against 'Math-RL-written draw 1 432 (+5.7 [2.6, 8.7]), draw 2 401 (-0.6 [-4.5, 3.2])'. Tokens per problem were 4,400 vs 4,361, a ratio of 1.01, so the length prior moved equally in both draws. The 28-problem difference therefore cannot come from 'the two sets differ in length'. The same holds for the base-written sets: draw 2 produced longer answers than draw 1 and did no better (result-6d422d '414/497 tokens 3380'; result-5227b9 '403/494 tokens 3741'). (2) Without length, the only channel left is the closing re-check, and the board rules that out too. result-855858: 'RL does not win by checking more' and 'markers do not separate right from wrong samples of the same model and problem'. result-882fa7: raising the base's Wait/check rate to RL's level gives '+0.5 pts [-2.2, +3.1]', and 'the push adds the word without a check'. (3) On hard328 the longer prior from the same draw-1 examples gave 'RL-written draw 1 164/328 vs 164 (0.0 [-4.3, 4.3]; 26 problems only with, 26 only without), cap hits 107 vs 77' (result-5227b9), so where answers did get longer there was no net gain. The mechanism's first test (median n_new of draw 1 over draw 2 >= 1.2, refuted below 1.05) is already implied to fail by the board's own mean-token figures (ratio 1.01). The draw-1 vs draw-2 difference has to come from something in the example texts other than their length, such as a copied answer: result-6d422d notes '2 RL-arm answers copy an example's answer'.

r8-m05.abandon: m05 needs the cued base's T 0.6 failures (loops on long problems) and its T 1.0 failures (finished wrong answers on short and medium problems) to fall on largely different problems. Its own starting item says they mostly fall on the same problems. knowledge-13cff3: T 0.6 finishes 402 problems with 378 right; resampling its 98 cap hits at T 1.0 gives 'Right of 500: 422, 424, 427, 432 (mean 426.2)', so a T 1.0 sample is right on only 44-54 of those 98 loop problems and wrong on 44-54 of them. The same item says 'on the 402 problems that finish at T 0.6, T 1.0 gets 361-364 against 378', so the same T 1.0 samples make only 38-41 errors on the other 402 problems. Per sample, more than half of T 1.0's ~90 errors sit on the 20 % of problems where T 0.6 loops. T 1.0's error rate there is about 45-55 %, against about 10 % elsewhere. Even if all ~22 T 1.0 cap hits per sample fell on those problems, at least 22 of T 1.0's ~68 finished-wrong answers per sample would be on them. The two temperatures fail on largely the same hard problems: the overlap is strongly positive, not disjoint. The length split is also contradicted. knowledge-9e4147: 'the cued-base gap to RL at T 1.0 is in every length quartile and largest on the longest problems', with 'cued base T1 111, 111, 99, 68' right of 125 by RL-length quartile. So T 1.0 loses most on the longest problems, not on short and medium ones. result-5e17a6 adds 'Base answers <= 2,000 tokens: 263, 13 wrong'. The recovery claim has no support either: knowledge-13cff3 says the hybrid's 'paired intervals include 0 in 10 of 12 sample pairings' and that the gain is under 2 points against the equal-effort T 1.0 restart. With the board's own counts, m05's first_test (cross-temperature union minus same-temperature union) comes out near -17 problems, not >= +8: about 434 for T 0.6 plus a T 1.0 sample against about 451 for two T 1.0 samples. That is because T 0.6 is right on fewer problems (378) and its losses lie where T 1.0 also fails. The vote shortfall of result-e41d94 therefore needs another cause, such as heterogeneous problem difficulty (33 problems at 0 of 4), not a second temperature axis.

r8-m06.abandon: The board already contradicts m06's core claim that the cued base loses its hold on the givens late in long answers, so that its gap to RL grows with position even on problems it has started correctly. (1) The prefix hand-off test measures this directly, and the base continuing late in an answer is as good as RL. result-a6ab7a: 'RL's advantage is in the first half of the answer and is in the text by the halfway point', 'Right prefixes from 50 % on: both finish equally (83 vs 83 of 88 base prefixes; 131 vs 134 of 140 RL prefixes)', and 'Refuted: 'late checking' (no RL edge at 75 %)'. From a sound prefix at 50 % or more, the base finishes as often as RL, and the base finishing RL's 75 % prefix recovers 17.5 of 21.3 points. If the givens faded with distance, the base would be the weaker finisher exactly in these late segments. (2) The observation m06 starts from, 'the gap rises with length even where neither model hits the cap', is not in the item it cites. knowledge-9e4147 says 'T1 cap hits exceed T2's by 15.2 points in Q4 and by 0-1.6 elsewhere'. So 15.2 of the 20.0-point Q4 gap is cap hits, and the finished-answer gap in Q4 (about 5 points) is smaller than in Q1-Q3 (about 9 to 14). (3) Wrong steps sit early, not late. result-afc423: 'First wrong step at median 0.20 of the answer'. result-c495fe: 'before a judged misreading it has already lost 32 points', so misreadings are set up early in the text. result-f3d708: 'misread samples do not have the lowest value' of problem dependence. A late drift of the givens predicts the opposite in each case.

r8-m07.abandon: m07 says the top directions of any GRPO-style RL-Zero delta write a reward-agnostic length prior that pulls every answer toward one target of a few thousand tokens, lengthening short answers and cutting long ones. The board already contradicts all three parts. (1) It is not reward-agnostic. The 8 directions of the General RL-Zero run, a GRPO run from the same recipe, do not finish answers: result-6f1bb7 reports 'General 164/88', i.e. 88 cap hits against the base's 77, where Math gives 46 and the dial goes down to 5. The whole IF delta also drives answers to almost no length, not to a few thousand tokens: result-edceef gives 'IF 55 (answers in a median of 5 tokens)'. The length these runs settle on depends on the reward. (2) There is no target of a few thousand tokens at which long answers are cut. In the item m07 starts from, result-1b6bf2, every quantile of finished length rises at 1x: 'top-8 1252/5513/14398 -> 1654/6094/14816', so p90 goes up, not down. For RL itself, 'RL 1295/6174/13532 -> 2401/7718/13532': p10 and p50 rise and p90 does not move. If there is a fixed point, it sits near 13-14k tokens, not between 2,500 and 8,000 as m07's first test requires. Only the 2x edit lowers p90 ('2x 1297/6409/14487 -> 2107/7088/12308'), and the 2x row is the over-dose regime. (3) The 'cuts long ones' half has no support other than cap hits being turned into finished answers. That is an end-of-answer effect, the additive hazard of m08, not a pull toward one length from both sides. So the same directions lengthen short answers and leave the tail in place or lengthen it.

r8-m08.abandon: m08 needs the RL delta to add a roughly fixed amount to the per-token log-odds of closing, whatever the host. Under its own exponential-hazard reading (P(cap) = exp(-h * 16,384), so ln h moves by the same amount in every host for the same dose), the board already says no. (1) The same full delta at a = 1 moves the two hosts very differently. Base -> RL: result-82b4dc 'base+cue 164/328 (50.0 %, 77 cap hits), RL 206/328 (62.8 %, 20 cap hits)'; RL is base + 1.0(RL - base), so ln h rises by ln(ln(328/20)/ln(328/77)) = 0.66. Think-SFT -> Think-SFT + 1.0(RL - base): result-3387ce 'cap hits 94.5, 75, 54, 44, 33 for a = 0..4', so ln h rises by ln(ln(328/75)/ln(328/94.5)) = 0.17. That is about 4 times less, not a fixed amount. (2) The two curves bend in opposite directions. Think-SFT's ln h rises 0.17, 0.20, 0.11, 0.13 per unit of a, which slows down. The base's finish dial (result-6f1bb7 '-1 118/96; base 164/77; 0.5 170/50; 1 192/46; 1.5 203/25', then '2 190/5') rises 0.30, 0.54, 0.97 per unit of a over 0->1, 1->1.5, 1.5->2, which speeds up. A fixed shift per unit of dose would make both straight lines, and the first_test's own R^2 >= 0.9 linearity is already in doubt. (3) The hosts' own hazards are too close to need double the dose. At a = 0, cap hits are 77 of 328 (base, cue) against 94.5 of 328 (Think-SFT); over 4 samples, result-fc7efc gives 'Cap hits: RL 114, base 286, Think-SFT 378'. With a fixed shift, Think-SFT needs only ln(1.449/1.244) = 0.15 more in ln h to reach any cap level the base reaches. That is about a quarter of the base's shift per unit dose, nowhere near twice the dose. (4) The ratio being explained compares two different vectors and an unresolved peak. The base peak is for the top-8 directions, not the full delta that Think-SFT got. result-6f1bb7 says itself that '1.5 was one of seven sizes tried' and '203 at size 1.5 against 192 at size 1 is +3.4 pts [-0.9, 7.6]', so 'peaks near 1.5' is not established. On the Think-SFT side, the a = 2 optimum was chosen on the 328 itself (result-3387ce: 'The coefficient was chosen on the 328 itself'). A theory built on transferring a fixed log-odds dose between hosts would spend tests on a premise the stored cap-hit counts already refute: the same delta buys the base about 4 times more ending hazard than it buys Think-SFT. Caveat: the RL reference in (1) is RL plain (206/20); RL cue scores 205 and its cap-hit count is not on the board.

r8-m11.abandon: The board already contradicts the mechanism's central claim that 'most of its cap hits are drifted traces'. result-818c20 counts the drift directly: 'Cap hits are unfinished reasoning, not loops (rule A 6 of 378; 86 switch into Chinese).' The denominator of 378 is Think-SFT's full set of cap hits over 4 samples on hard328 (result-fc7efc: 'Cap hits: RL 114, base 286, Think-SFT 378'). So only 86/378 = 0.23 of the cap hits drift into Chinese. That is far below 'most', and the mechanism's own first test (share of cap hits that drift >= 0.5) is already failed by a number on the board. Because of this, drift cannot explain the observation the mechanism was built for: neither finisher rescues Think-SFT's cap-hit prefixes. In result-bce075, 'On Think-SFT's 89 cap-hit prefixes RL as finisher has 18 and 17 right, Think 18 and 16', and RL makes them finish but wrongly: '59 to 65 of the 89 become wrong boxed answers'. At a 23 % drift share, at least about three quarters of those prefixes stay in English and still are not rescued. So the failure to rescue is general to Think-SFT's cap hits, not specific to a drift state. result-b006f5 points instead to problem difficulty as the cause: 'RL's precision on the 141 problems with a Think-SFT cap hit is 31.2 %, against 35.2 % expected from the base's solve rate: mostly difficulty'. In result-3387ce the RL delta's effect ('The RL change makes Think-SFT finish: cap hits 94.5, 75, 54, 44, 33 for a = 0..4, while right-of-finished falls 88 to 72 %') is a general push to finish. It fits the finish dial of result-6f1bb7 and result-51a0e7, which works the same way on the English-only base, so suppressing language drift is not needed to explain it. Drift into Chinese is a real minority feature of the cap hits (about 23 %). It is not the mechanism behind them, and a theory built on it would spend tests on a cause the board has already measured as minor.
